title: Evaluative verdict on someone's reaction/behavior
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic evaluative judgments about a person's reaction, response, or behavior, typically in advice/AITA-style contexts, using a possessive subject (e.g., 'Your dad's reaction', 'Her response') followed by a copular evaluation like 'unacceptable', 'unfair', 'understandable but harsh', 'disproportionate', or 'concerning'. It activates most strongly on terse, standalone sentences that render a clear moral/emotional verdict on someone's conduct, often with a concessive structure ('while understandable, ... is also unfair'). It does NOT activate on longer advice, explanations, suggestions, or descriptive narrative sentences that don't deliver a compact judgment on a specific party's reaction or behavior, nor on generic supportive statements, questions, or procedural/list-formatting text lacking an evaluative verdict.

title: Advice-giving list/method markers
description: This latent fires on the structural scaffolding of relationship/interpersonal advice: numbered list markers ("2.", "3.", "4."), sentence-initial method prepositions like "By" or "Try to" that introduce a recommended action, and imperative openers ("Consider", "Practice", "Be patient", "Seek support") that begin a suggested strategy, especially ones invoking open/honest communication. It activates most strongly on these short fragmentary openers and enumerators themselves, even in isolation, rather than on the full elaborated advice sentence. It does not activate strongly on descriptive, evaluative, or narrative sentences that lack this list/method-introducing syntax (e.g., statements assessing blame, expressing empathy, or describing a situation) even if they discuss the same relationship-advice topic.

title: Conversational rapport-building questions and advice
description: This latent fires on conversational scripts and social-coaching content: short questions one might ask in small talk or networking ('What do you like about it?', 'Would you like to exchange numbers?', 'What do you do in your free time?') and related advice for making conversation, initiating contact, or engaging with someone (asking follow-up questions, avoiding rambling, suggesting activities like coffee or joining a group). It activates on second-person interrogatives and imperative tips aimed at facilitating social interaction, friendship-building, or self-improvement discussions (hobbies, interests, small talk topics), as well as reassuring statements normalizing awkwardness or effort in these situations. It does NOT activate on purely factual, narrative, or technical statements lacking this direct interpersonal/conversational framing, nor on questions that aren't oriented toward eliciting personal preference, interest, or social connection (e.g., abstract or expository content unrelated to dialogue or advice-giving).

title: Enumerating possible options via or-questions
description: This latent fires on sentences that lay out a small set of alternative possibilities—usually as an 'X, Y, or Z' question or speculative list—to narrow down an ambiguous situation or invite the reader to specify which case applies (e.g., 'Are they tired?', 'A friend, coworker, acquaintance, or someone you've met online?', 'Was it a casual encounter, a work meeting, or a social event?'). It also activates on related brainstorming/suggestion fragments that hedge over multiple candidate answers or advice items ('They might know of someone...', 'The motorist may have been distracted, tired, or simply made a mistake'). It does not activate on flat declarative statements, single-answer factual claims, or questions that have only one clear referent with no listed alternatives, since the defining feature is the enumerative 'or'-based hedging/clarifying structure rather than the topic being discussed.

title: Exclamatory naming of a familiar problem
description: This latent fires on short, punchy phrases that label a common, relatable struggle or dilemma, typically using stock intensifiers like "age-old," "eternal," "classic," or "pesky" and ending in an exclamation point (e.g., "The age-old dilemma!", "The pesky problem of procrastinating!"). It activates on sentences that function as a rhetorical framing device—introducing a topic by naming it as a universally recognized issue before elaborating—rather than on sentences that actually explain, argue, or describe solutions in depth. It also weakly extends to related routine/habit-building tips that follow such framings, but the core trigger is the exclamatory labeling construction itself. It would not activate on neutral, declarative statements of fact, technical explanations, or sentences that discuss a problem without the characteristic "stock-phrase + exclamation" framing (e.g., "HSV causes recurring outbreaks" activates weakly or via other latents rather than this pattern).

title: Exclamatory naming of a familiar trope
description: This latent fires on short, sentence-fragment exclamations that spotlight a well-known, relatable phenomenon by naming it with a colorful epithet (e.g., 'elusive', 'infamous') followed by an exclamation point, often relying on a noun phrase rather than a full clause. It captures a rhetorical move of wryly labeling a shared cultural or experiential concept ('the freshman slump!', 'the college dance party experience!') as if invoking a common trope the reader will recognize. It also extends loosely to statements pushing back on assumed social hierarchies tied to such tropes (e.g., debunking prestige assumptions about colleges). It would not activate on plain, declarative descriptions of the same topics that lack the punchy, fragment-like exclamatory framing or the ironic 'everyone knows this' tone.

title: Numbered list markers
description: This latent fires on standalone numerals (often followed by a period or bold markdown asterisks) that serve as list-item or enumeration markers, such as '2.', '3.', '4. **', etc. It activates most strongly on isolated digit tokens that begin or delimit a numbered list item, largely independent of the surrounding topic or content. It also weakly activates on similar numeral markers embedded within longer advice-style sentences that are part of numbered lists. It would not activate on sentences that merely mention numbers as part of ordinary prose content (e.g., quantities, percentages, dates) or on list items lacking an explicit numeral marker, since the trigger is specifically the enumerating digit token itself rather than the semantic content of the list.

title: Empathetic framing of relatable everyday struggles
description: This latent fires on short, conversational statements that validate or name a common, relatable everyday difficulty or aspiration—often framed with an exclamation or a generalizing phrase like 'the eternal struggle of...', 'the allure of...', or 'it can be debilitating/exhausting...'. It also activates on brief affirming/acknowledging responses ('That's a great observation!', 'Yes, that's a common phenomenon') and on small, practical tips framed as manageable fixes to such struggles (e.g., 'Commit to 2 minutes', 'save $5-10 a day'). It captures a rhetorical stance of sympathetic recognition of a widely-shared minor hardship or desire, paired with an implicit invitation toward small remedies. It would NOT activate on purely factual, technical, or neutral descriptive statements (e.g., a scoring formula explanation) that lack this empathetic, relatable-struggle framing, nor on sentences that state facts without any evaluative or validating tone.

title: Listicle tip header with imperative action
description: This latent fires on entries in a tip/advice list where a short imperative action phrase (often bolded, ending in '**') is followed by a colon and a brief explanatory clause elaborating on the rationale or method. It activates on the structural pattern of 'Do X**: explanation of why/how' typical of numbered self-help, productivity, or habit-formation lists, regardless of the specific topic (health, finance, lifestyle, etc.). It would not activate on plain narrative sentences, general advice given without the bolded-imperative-plus-colon list format, or standalone imperative commands lacking the following explanatory clause.

title: List-item generalization opener
description: This latent fires on short, standalone sentences that function as generalized opening statements or bullet points in advice-style or listicle writing, often making broad claims about people's expectations, traits, or capabilities ('Not everyone...', 'Expect you to...'). It responds to the rhetorical pattern of a terse, declarative generalization that introduces or summarizes a point, frequently the first sentence of a list entry or paragraph, including even a bare imperative fragment like 'Put' that signals the start of such an item. It would not activate on detailed, context-rich narrative sentences, technical explanations, or sentences embedded mid-argument that elaborate rather than introduce a generalized claim.
